source_text: De exitu plane, puto, diuersitatem temptatis inducere, negantes passionem crucis in Christum creatoris praedicatam et argumentantes insuper non esse credendum, ut in id genus mortis exposuerit creator filium suum, quod ipse maledixerat: maledictus, inquit, omnis qui pependerit in ligno. sed huius maledictionis sensum differo digne a sola praedicatione crucis, de qua nunc maxime quaeritur, quia et alias antecedit rerum probatio rationem. de figuris prius edocebo. et utique uel maxime sacramentum istud figurari in praedicatione oportebat, quanto incredibile, tanto magis scandalo futurum. si nude praedicaretur, quantoque magnificum, tanto magis obumbrandum, ut difficultas intellectus gratiam dei quaereret. itaque inprimis Isaac, cum a patre in hostiam deditus lignum sibi portaret ipse, Christi exitum iam tunc denotabat, in uictimam concessi a patre et lignum passionis suae baiulantis. Ioseph. et ipse Christum figuraturus, uel hoc solo, ne demorer cursum. quod persecutionem a fratribus passus est ob dei gratiam. sicut et Christus a Iudaeis carnaliter (fratribus,) cum benedicitur a patre etiam in haec uerba: tauri decor eius, cornua unicornis cornua eius, in eis nationes uentilabit pariter ad summum usque terrae, non utique rhinoceros destinabatur unicornis nec minotaurus bicornis, sed Christus in illo significabatur, taurus ob utramque dispositionem, aliis ferus ut iudex, aliis mansuetus ut saluator, cuius cornua essent crucis extima. nam et in antemna, quae crucis pars est, extremitates cornua uocantur, unicornis autem mediae stipitis palus. hac denique uirtute crucis et hoc more cornutus uniuersas gentes et nunc uentilat per fidem, auferens a terra in caelum, et tunc per iudicium uentilabit, deiciens de caelo in terram. idem erit et alibi taurus apud eandem scripturam, cum Iacob in Simeonem et Leui, id est in scribas et Pharisaeos, — ex illis enim deducitur census. istorum — spiritaliter imprecatur: Simeon et Leui perfecerunt iniquitatem ex sua haeresi, qua scilicet Christum sunt persecuti; in consilium eorum ne uenerit anima mea et in stationem eorum ne incubuerint iecora mea, quia in indignatione sua interfecerunt homines, id est prophetas, et in concupiscentia sua ceciderunt neruos tauro, id est Christo, quem post necem prophetarum suffigendo neruos utique eius clauis desaeuierunt. ceterum uanum, si post homicidia alicuius bouis illis exprobrat carnificinam. iam uero Moyses, quid utique tunc tantum, cum Iesus aduersus Amalech proeliabatur, expansis manibus orat residens, quando in rebus tam attonitis magis utique genibus depositis et manibus caedentibus pectus et facie humi uolutante orationem commendare debuisset, nisi quia illic, ubi nomen domini dimicabat, dimicaturi quandoque aduersus diabolum, crucis quoque erat habitus necessarius, per quam Iesus uictoriam esset relaturus? idem rursus Moyses post interdictam omnis rei similitudinem cur aereum serpentem ligno impositum pendentis habitu in spectaculum salutare proposuit? an et hic dominicae crucis uim intentabat, qua serpens diabolus publicabatur et laeso cuique a spiritalibus colubris, intuenti tamen et credenti in eam, sanitas morsuum peccatorum et salus exinde praedicabatur?
pass_a_gloss: Concerning the outcome, I think, you are trying to introduce a difference, denying the passion of the cross preached in Christ of the creator and arguing, furthermore, that it is not to be believed that the creator exposed his son to this kind of death, which he himself had cursed, saying, 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.' But I put off the sense of this curse, worthy of consideration, from the sole preaching of the cross, which is now most in question, because the proof of things also precedes the argument in other matters. First, I will teach about the figures. And certainly, or rather, this sacrament had to be figured in the preaching, as much as it was incredible, so much the more it was going to be a scandal, and if it were preached naked, as much as it was magnificent, so much the more it was going to be obscured, so that the difficulty of understanding might seek the grace of God. Therefore, first of all, Isaac, when he was given by his father as a sacrifice and carried the wood himself, already then denoted the outcome of Christ, having been given as a victim by his father and carrying the wood of his passion. And Joseph, he too figures Christ, or at least in this one thing, lest I delay the course. What he suffered, persecution from his brothers, on account of the grace of God. Just as Christ also suffered from the Jews, in a carnal manner, from brothers, when he is blessed by the father, even in these words: 'The beauty of his horns is like that of a unicorn, with his horns he will gore the nations, even to the ends of the earth.' Not, indeed, was the rhinoceros or the two-horned minotaur destined to be the unicorn, but Christ was signified in it, a bull on account of both dispositions, fierce to some as a judge, gentle to others as a savior, whose horns were the extremities of the cross. For even in the yardarm, which is a part of the cross, the extremities are called horns, but the unicorn is the middle pole. By this virtue of the cross and in this manner, horned, he now wins over all nations through faith, taking them away from the earth to heaven, and then he will win them over through judgment, casting them down from heaven to earth. The same will be true elsewhere, the bull, in the same scripture, when Jacob spiritually curses Simeon and Levi, that is, the scribes and Pharisees - for the census of these is derived from them - saying: 'Simeon and Levi have completed iniquity from their own heresy, by which, indeed, they persecuted Christ; may my soul not come into their counsel and may my liver not incubate in their station, because in their indignation they killed men, that is, prophets, and in their concupiscence they struck the sinews of the bull, that is, Christ, whom, after the death of the prophets, they certainly crucified, nailing his sinews.' But it is vain, if after the homicides of someone's ox, he reproaches them for butchery. Now, indeed, Moses - what, indeed, then, when Jesus was fighting against Amalech, with his hands spread out, praying, sitting - when in such astonishing matters, he ought to have commended the prayer, rather, with his knees deposited and his hands beating his chest and his face rolling on the ground, unless because, there, where the name of the Lord was fighting, those who would fight against the devil were also to fight, and the habit of the cross was necessary, through which Jesus was going to relate the victory? The same Moses, again, after every likeness of anything was forbidden, why did he propose a bronze serpent, imposed on wood, in a hanging habit, as a spectacle of salvation? Or did he also intend the power of the Lord's cross, by which the serpent, the devil, was made public, and to each one wounded by spiritual serpents, yet looking at and believing in it, health from the bites of sins and salvation was preached from then on?

pass_b_english: You are trying to drive a wedge into the outcome, I think, denying that the passion of the cross was preached in Christ of the Creator, and arguing further that we should not believe the Creator exposed his Son to this kind of death, since he himself cursed it: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree" (Deuteronomy 21:23). But I set aside the sense of this curse, which deserves careful handling, from the bare preaching of the cross—the very point now under fire—because the proof of things precedes argument in other matters as well. First, I will teach the figures.

And this sacrament had to be foreshadowed in the preaching precisely because the more incredible it was, the more it would become a scandal; and the more magnificent it was, the more it had to be veiled if preached nakedly, so that the difficulty of understanding might drive people to seek the grace of God. So first, Isaac: when his father gave him as a sacrifice and he carried the wood himself, he already signified Christ's outcome—handed over as a victim by his Father, bearing the wood of his own passion. And Joseph, too, figures Christ—if only in this one thing, lest I delay the argument: he suffered persecution from his brothers on account of the grace of God, just as Christ suffered from the Jews, carnally his brothers.

When the Father blesses him in these words—"The beauty of his horns is like that of a unicorn; with his horns he will gore the nations, even to the ends of the earth"—no rhinoceros or two-horned minotaur was destined to be the unicorn, but Christ was signified in it, a bull on account of both dispositions: fierce to some as judge, gentle to others as savior, whose horns are the extremities of the cross. For even on the yardarm, which is a part of the cross, the extremities are called horns, while the unicorn is the middle pole. By this virtue of the cross and in this horned manner, he now gathers all nations through faith, lifting them from earth to heaven, and then he will gather them through judgment, casting them down from heaven to earth.

The same holds true elsewhere in the same Scripture, when Jacob spiritually curses Simeon and Levi—that is, the scribes and Pharisees, for their census derives from them—saying: "Simeon and Levi have completed iniquity from their own heresy, by which they persecuted Christ; may my soul not come into their counsel, and may my liver not rest in their assembly, because in their indignation they killed men—that is, prophets—and in their concupiscence they struck the sinews of the bull, that is, Christ, whom, after the death of the prophets, they crucified by nailing his sinews." But it is vain to reproach them with butchery after the homicides of someone's ox.

Now, what was Moses doing at that moment when Jesus fought Amalek, praying with hands spread wide while seated? In such an astonishing crisis, he ought rather to have fallen on his knees, beating his chest, rolling his face on the ground—unless, in the place where the Name of the Lord was doing battle, those who would someday fight the devil also needed the posture of the cross, through which Jesus would carry off the victory. And again, after every likeness of anything was forbidden, why did Moses set up a bronze serpent on a pole, hung as a spectacle of salvation? Was he not also intending the power of the Lord's cross, by which the serpent, the devil, was exposed, and by which, to each one wounded by spiritual serpents, yet looking at it and believing in it, healing from the bites of sins and salvation were proclaimed from then on? (Numbers 21:9)
